entry: Island and unitary authority off the south coast of England (est. pop., 2024: 141,660). Separated from the mainland by the Solent strait and otherwise surrounded by the [[English Channel]], it is the largest island in England, with 380 sq km (150 sq mi) of land. It was historically part of [[Hampshire]]. The largely rural island is said to be the sunniest place in Great Britain and has been designated a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve. Victorian-era tourism developed there, and [[Queen Victoria]] built Osborne House at East Cowes. Its maritime and industrial tradition includes boat-building, sail-making, flying boats and [[Hovercraft|hovercraft]].

Small archipelago in Cornwall, England, about 45 km (28 mi) southwest of Land's End, with a population of 2,100 at the 2021 [[United Kingdom]] census. People have lived there since at least the [[Iron Age]]. The islands were a Royalist base during the [[English Civil War]] until Parliament captured them in 1651. In 1707, four Royal Navy ships were wrecked off the islands, and at least 1,450 people died. The islands are known for pilot gig racing, and rock climbing on the [[Granite|granite]] coast has been practiced since 1977. [[Tourism]] is a major part of the economy.

Khedive of [[Egypt]] and Sudan, 1863–1879, also known as Ismail the Magnificent. Sharing the outlook of his grandfather, Muhammad Ali Pasha, he invested heavily in industry, [[Urbanization|urbanization]] and the expansion of the country's boundaries in Africa. He built over 900 miles (1,400 km) of railroads and 4,500 schools. In 1867 he paid the [[Ottoman Empire|Ottoman]] sultan for recognition of his title of khedive, with succession passing only to his direct descendants. His spending, including much of the money for the [[Suez Canal]], left the khedivate deeply in debt, and Egypt's shares in the Suez Canal Company were sold to the British government. He was removed in 1879 under British and French pressure. The city of Ismailia is named in his honor.

Founder and first shah of [[Safavid Iran]], ruling 1501–1524. Ismail inherited leadership of the Safavid Sufi order as a child and was crowned shah in 1501, with [[Tabriz]] as the capital. His expansion into eastern [[Anatolia]] brought conflict with the [[Ottoman Empire]], which decisively defeated the Safavids at the Battle of Chaldiran in 1514. He made [[Shia Islam|Twelver Shia Islam]] the official religion of the Safavid state, a turning point in the history of Islam. In 1508 he destroyed the tombs of the Abbasid caliphs, Abu Hanifa and Abdul Qadir Gilani, causing sectarian tensions in the [[Middle East]]. He was also a prolific poet, writing in a southern Turkic dialect under the pen name Khaṭāʾī.

Albanian novelist, poet, essayist and playwright. Living under strict censorship in Albania, he used parable, myth, [[Fable|fable]], folk-tale and allegory to outwit Communist censors, who had banned three of his books. His first novel, *The General of the Dead Army*, made him famous internationally. In 1990 he defected to Paris to escape the Communist regime and its Sigurimi secret police. A Neustadt Prize juror called him the successor of [[Franz Kafka]], and some regard him as a universal voice against [[Totalitarianism|totalitarianism]]. He was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature 15 times and won the 2005 inaugural Man Booker International Prize. In 2023 he was granted citizenship of [[Kosovo]].

Structure-preserving, reversible mapping between two mathematical structures of the same type. Isomorphic structures share the same properties with respect to the structure considered, so they may often be identified. The term is mainly used for [[Algebraic structure|algebraic structures]] and [[Category theory|categories]], where a homomorphism is an isomorphism if and only if it is bijective. Specialized names include an isometry for [[Metric space|metric spaces]], a homeomorphism for [[Topological space|topological spaces]], and a permutation as an automorphism of a set. The [[Logarithm|logarithm]] is an isomorphism that translates multiplication of positive real numbers into addition of real numbers.

Colorless, flammable [[Organic compound|organic compound]], the simplest secondary alcohol. It is miscible with [[Water|water]], ethanol and chloroform, and adding sodium chloride separates it from salt solutions in a process called salting out. It forms an azeotrope with water. First synthesized in 1853 by Alexander William Williamson, it is made by hydration of propene or hydrogenation of [[Acetone|acetone]]. It serves as rubbing alcohol, hand sanitizer and solvent, and more than a million tonnes are produced annually. Its flammability and potential for peroxide formation pose risks, and ingestion can cause [[Central nervous system|central nervous system]] depression and [[Coma|coma]].

Admiral of the Imperial Japanese Navy and commander of its Combined Fleet during World War II. After graduating from the naval academy in 1904, he lost two fingers at the Battle of Tsushima in the [[Russo-Japanese War]]. He studied at [[Harvard University]] and served as naval attaché in Washington, concluding that naval aviation and [[Aircraft carrier|aircraft carriers]] would be decisive. He opposed war with the United States, but as commander-in-chief from 1939 he conceived the initial surprise [[Attack on Pearl Harbor|attack on Pearl Harbor]]. Japan's early naval victories were halted at the [[Battle of Midway]] in June 1942, where four Japanese carriers were sunk. He could not prevent the loss of the Solomon Islands in the [[Guadalcanal campaign]]. American code breakers intercepted his flight plans, and his aircraft was shot down over [[New Guinea]].

Nuclear species of the same [[Chemical element|chemical element]], with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Isotopes have virtually the same chemical properties but different atomic masses and physical properties. The name, from Greek roots meaning equal and place, reflects that they occupy the same place on the [[Periodic table|periodic table]]. Margaret Todd suggested the term in 1913 to Frederick Soddy, who popularized it. The [[Atomic number|atomic number]] is fixed for an element, while the mass number is the total of its [[Proton|protons]] and neutrons. For example, [[Carbon|carbon]]-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14 have 6, 7 and 8 neutrons. Some isotopes are radioactive, and [[Technetium|technetium-99m]] is used in medical imaging.

National military of [[Israel]]. Formed on May 26, 1948, on the orders of [[David Ben-Gurion]], it drew its initial recruits from pre-state paramilitaries. After the 1979 and 1994 peace treaties with Egypt and Jordan, it refocused on southern Lebanon and the Palestinian territories, withdrawing from southern Lebanon in 2000 and Gaza in 2005. It is believed to have had an operational [[Nuclear weapon|nuclear weapons]] capability since 1967. Its actions in the Palestinian territories have drawn criticism, and multiple human rights organizations and scholars accuse it of [[Genocide|genocide]].

American musician and singer from [[Hawaii]], also called Braddah IZ. He is regarded as one of Hawaii's greatest musicians, and he incorporated [[Jazz|jazz]] and [[Reggae|reggae]] into his ukulele playing. In 2010 [[NPR]] named him one of its 50 Great Voices, calling him "The Voice of Hawaii." His 1993 studio [[Album|album]] *Facing Future* brought mainstream popularity. His medley "Somewhere Over the Rainbow/What a Wonderful World" spent 375 weeks on top of the World Digital Songs chart, the longest-leading number-one hit on any Billboard song chart.

Ongoing military and political conflict over land and self-determination in the former territory of [[Mandatory Palestine]]. It originated with the Zionist movement's aim of establishing a Jewish state through colonization, and the 1917 [[Balfour Declaration]] promised support for a "Jewish homeland" in Palestine. After the United Nations proposed partitioning the territory in 1947, a plan that Arab leaders rejected, civil war broke out. In the 1948 Palestine war Israel was founded, and more than half of the Palestinian Arab population fled or was expelled, an event Palestinians call the [[Nakba]]. Since the Six-Day War of 1967, Israel has occupied the [[West Bank]] and [[Gaza Strip]]. The [[International Court of Justice]] ruled in July 2024 that Israel continues to occupy them illegally. Attacks by [[Hamas]] in October 2023 killed nearly 1,200 people, and the war that followed has caused widespread destruction and famine in Gaza.

Semitic-speaking people of ancient [[Canaan]] during the [[Iron Age]]. They are associated with the Hebrews, and they founded the two Iron Age kingdoms of Israel and Judah. According to the Bible, they were twelve related tribes. Their religion centered on [[Yahweh]], an ancient Semitic god. The [[Neo-Assyrian Empire]] conquered Israel around 720 BCE, and the Neo-Babylonian Empire conquered Judah around 586 BCE. Modern descendants include [[Jews]] and Samaritans.

Endorheic saline lake in the [[Tian Shan]] mountains of eastern [[Kyrgyzstan]]. At 1,607 m (5,272 ft) above sea level, it is the eighth-deepest lake in the world, the eleventh-largest by volume, and the second-largest saline lake. It is 182 km (113 mi) long and reaches a depth of 668 m (2,192 ft). It is the second-largest mountain lake in the world, behind [[Lake Titicaca]] in [[South America]], and its high salinity keeps it from freezing even in winter. About 118 rivers and streams flow into it, and it has no current outlet. The lake is a Ramsar site and part of the Issyk-Kul Biosphere Reserve. A stop on the [[Silk Road]], it was noted by the Buddhist scholar-monk [[Xuanzang]] in the 7th century. It was later ceded to Russia under the Treaty of Tarbagatai, and during the Soviet era it became a popular resort.

Narrow strip of land connecting two larger landmasses across an expanse of water. The word comes from the Ancient Greek for neck. Its inverse counterpart is a [[Strait|strait]], a narrow stretch of sea between two landmasses. The Isthmus of Panama is crossed by the [[Panama Canal]], which connects the [[Atlantic Ocean]] and [[Pacific Ocean]]. The Isthmus of Suez, formed by the [[Sinai Peninsula]], is cut by the [[Suez Canal]], linking the [[Mediterranean Sea]] and [[Red Sea]]. Canals are often built across isthmuses as shortcuts for shipping.

Japanese statesman and first prime minister of Japan, 1885–1888. Born into a poor farming family, he was adopted into a low-ranking [[Samurai|samurai]] family and studied in England. As a senior member of the genrō, he led the drafting of the 1889 Meiji Constitution, which was modeled on that of Prussia and reserved considerable power for the emperor. He served three more terms as prime minister between 1892 and 1901 and founded the Rikken Seiyūkai party in 1900. After the Russo-Japanese War he became the first Resident-General of [[Korea]] and eventually supported annexation. He was assassinated by a Korean nationalist in [[Harbin]], [[Manchuria]], four months after resigning that post.

1986 horror novel by American author [[Stephen King]]. Seven outcast children, the Losers' Club, are terrorized in Derry, Maine, by a shapeshifting entity called It, which often appears as Pennywise the Dancing Clown. The entity awakens every 27 years, and the children return as adults to confront it. The nonlinear narrative alternates between the late 1950s and adulthood, exploring memory, childhood trauma and the loss of innocence. *It* was the best-selling hardcover fiction book in the United States in 1986, and Pennywise has become one of the most iconic villains in [[Popular culture|popular culture]].

American [[Sitcom|sitcom]] that premiered on FX in 2005. *It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia* follows self-centered friends who run Paddy's Pub, a struggling Irish dive bar in South Philadelphia. Their elaborate schemes against outsiders and one another, for gain or revenge, usually fail. Created by Rob McElhenney and co-developed by Glenn Howerton, it is the longest-running American live-action sitcom in total seasons. Critics praise its [[Dark humor|dark humor]] and [[Satire|satire]] of racism, [[Misogyny|misogyny]], [[Homophobia|homophobia]] and other prejudices.

1946 American Christmas fantasy drama directed by [[Frank Capra]]. *It's a Wonderful Life* stars [[James Stewart]] as George Bailey, a man who gives up his dreams to help others and contemplates suicide on Christmas Eve. His guardian angel shows him what the world would be like had he never lived. Adapted from a short story loosely based on Dickens's *A Christmas Carol*, it was nominated for five [[Academy Awards]], including Best Picture, but was a box-office disappointment. It became a Christmas classic after its copyright lapsed in 1974. It was selected in 1990 for preservation by the [[Library of Congress]].

Hydroelectric dam on the [[Paraná River]] at the border between [[Brazil]] and [[Paraguay]]. Its 20 generating units, each providing 700 MW, give an installed capacity of 14 GW. As of 2020 its power plant was the second-largest hydroelectric producer in the world, surpassed only by the [[Three Gorges Dam]] in China. The dam is operated jointly by the two countries through Itaipu Binacional, established under a 1973 treaty. Its construction displaced 10,000 families and flooded the Guaíra Falls. Ten generators run at 50 Hz for Paraguay and ten at 60 Hz for Brazil, and two 600 kV lines carry most of the energy to southeastern Brazil.

Series of European conflicts from 1494 to 1559, centered on the Italian Peninsula. The wars grew out of the French–Habsburg rivalry, pitting [[France]] against [[Spain]] and the [[Holy Roman Empire]], with Italian states, England and the [[Ottoman Empire]] involved at various stages. After the collapse of the Italic League in 1492, Charles VIII of France invaded Naples in 1494, drawing in Spain and the Holy Roman Empire. After 1503 most fighting came from French invasions of [[Lombardy]] and [[Piedmont]]. Growing Protestantism led the major belligerents to focus on religious conflict at home by 1557. The Treaty of Cateau-Cambrésis largely expelled France from Italy, and Spain gained the Kingdom of Naples, the [[Kingdom of Sicily]] and the Duchy of Milan. The wars are seen as a turning point toward modern warfare, marked by the spread of the [[Arquebus|arquebus]].

Mediterranean culinary tradition developed in [[Italy]] since Roman times and spread worldwide with Italian emigration. It is one of the best-known cuisines, and its emphasis on simplicity means many dishes use few ingredients of high quality. Many dishes were created by ordinary people rather than chefs. The introduction of [[Tomato|tomatoes]], potatoes and maize from the [[New World]] changed it significantly. The Mediterranean diet forms its basis, rich in [[Pasta|pasta]], fish, fruit and vegetables, with cheese, cold cuts and wine central. [[Tiramisu]] and gelato are among its famous desserts. Italy is the world's largest wine producer, and in 2025 [[UNESCO]] listed Italian cuisine as intangible cultural heritage.

Theater of [[World War I]] along the border between the [[Kingdom of Italy]] and [[Austria-Hungary]], 1915–1918. Italy had been allied with Germany and Austria-Hungary but entered the war on the Entente side, seeking Trento, Trieste, [[South Tyrol]] and Istria. Britain, France and Russia had secretly promised these territories in the 1915 Treaty of London. The front bogged down into [[Trench warfare|trench warfare]], with fighting at high altitudes in the [[Dolomites]] and the [[Karst]], and several thousand civilians died in refugee camps. Italian forces captured Trento and Trieste, and the war ended with the armistice of Villa Giusti on 4 November 1918. Treaties of 1919 and 1920 gave Italy Trento, Trieste, South Tyrol and Istria. Some historians regard the war as the completion of the [[Unification of Italy|unification of Italy]].

Romance language of the Indo-European family, descended from [[Latin]]. It is a standardized form of literary Florentine [[Tuscany|Tuscan]] and, with Sardinian, the least differentiated Romance language from Latin by most measures. An estimated 68 to 85 million people speak Italian, about 64 million as native speakers as of 2024. It is an official language in Italy, San Marino, Switzerland and Vatican City, and the main working language of the [[Holy See]]. It is the third-most-widely spoken native language in the [[European Union]]. Its loanwords are widely used in fashion, cuisine and musical terminology, including in [[Opera|opera]]. Almost all native Italian words end with [[Vowel|vowels]].

Literature written in the [[Italian language]], particularly within [[Italy]]. It began in the 12th century, when the vernacular was first used literarily, and the Ritmo laurenziano is the earliest extant document. Renaissance [[Humanism|humanism]] developed in the 14th and early 15th centuries, with [[Lorenzo de' Medici]] regarded as the standard bearer of Florence's influence. [[Niccolò Machiavelli]] and Francesco Guicciardini were the chief originators of the science of history. In the 18th century, Giuseppe Parini led a literary revival during the Age of Enlightenment. Alessandro Manzoni was the main instigator of the Romantic reform, and Giacomo Leopardi was the great poet of the age. Umberto Eco became internationally successful with *Il nome della rosa* (1980). Italian-language authors have won the Nobel Prize in Literature six times, as of 2019.
